title: Review: Indicators; Entropy; Gibbs free energy and feasibility; ΔG, K and Q; Electrolysis (molten and aqueous); Commercial cells and fuel cells; Electrode potentials and the SHE; Cell potentials and feasibility
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EN09#t1 term and clue written for the game; RX05#t1 term and clue written for the game; RX07#t1 term and clue written for the game; RX07#t3 term and clue written for the game. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Gibbs energy
items.clue: The quantity ΔG; it is zero when T = ΔH/ΔS and says nothing about rate.

items.label: Cell potential
items.clue: The gap between two E° values, e.g. +0.80 − (−0.76) = +1.56 V for silver with zinc.

items.label: Electrolytic cell
items.clue: Set-up in which a DC power supply drives a change that would not happen on its own.

items.label: Anode
items.clue: Where electrons are pulled out; the non-metal forms here from a molten binary salt.

questions.stem: An acid-base indicator, HIn, is yellow, and its conjugate base, In⁻, is blue. In a solution of pH 5.40 at 25°C, absorbance measurements show that [In⁻] is three times [HIn]. What is the pKa of HIn?
questions.explanation: Ka = [H₃O⁺][In⁻]/[HIn] = 10⁻⁵·⁴⁰ × 3 = 1.19 × 10⁻⁵, so pKa = 4.92. pH above pKa fits blue In⁻ predominating.

questions.stem: A hot metal block is pressed against an identical cold one. Energy flows from hot to cold until both are at the same temperature. It never flows back to make one block hot again. Why?

options.text: Cold flows from the cold block into the hot block until both reach the same temperature.
Energy shared over both blocks has vastly more possible arrangements, so total entropy rises.
Atoms from the hot block move across into the cold block, carrying their extra energy with them.
The hot block's entropy increases as it loses energy, so the flow keeps going.

questions.explanation: Shared between both blocks, the energy has far more possible arrangements. Concentrating it back into one block would lower the total entropy: overwhelmingly unlikely.

options.text: −257.2 kJ/mol_rxn

questions.stem: Molten zinc chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at each electrode?

options.text: Cathode: chlorine. Anode: zinc.
Cathode: zinc. Anode: chlorine.
Cathode: zinc. Anode: oxygen.
Cathode: Zn²⁺ ions. Anode: Cl⁻ ions, as the current splits the zinc chloride.

questions.explanation: Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn at the cathode; 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ at the anode. Metal at the cathode, non-metal at the anode.

questions.stem: Methyl orange can be written HInd(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + Ind⁻(aq), with HInd red and Ind⁻ yellow. A few drops are added to aqueous ammonia: the solution is yellow. Hydrochloric acid is run in. Near the end it turns orange, then red. Why?

options.text: Added H⁺ shifts the indicator equilibrium to the right, so the red Ind⁻ form builds up.
Once the ammonia is used up, added H⁺ shifts the equilibrium left, so red HInd builds up.
The indicator reacts with the ammonium chloride formed, making a red salt.
The solution turns red at exactly pH 7, when the ammonia is neutralised.

questions.explanation: While NH₃ remains, it mops up the H⁺. Past equivalence [H⁺] jumps, the pH falls through methyl orange's range, and [HInd]/[Ind⁻] = [H⁺]/Ka becomes large.

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, which half-reaction happens at the anode?

options.text: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb
Br₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Br⁻
Pb → Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻
2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻

questions.explanation: Br⁻ ions move to the anode and lose electrons (oxidation), forming bromine vapour.

questions.stem: Aluminium is made by electrolysing aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃. It is first dissolved in molten cryolite at about 950°C. Why can't solid Al₂O₃ simply be electrolysed?

options.text: Solid Al₂O₃ contains no ions until it is heated.
Solid Al₂O₃ has no free electrons to carry the current.
In the solid, the Al³⁺ and O²⁻ ions are fixed in the lattice and can't move to the electrodes.
Electrolysis needs heat, and the heat makes the reaction favored.

questions.explanation: Ions must reach the electrodes to be reduced (Al³⁺ at the cathode) or oxidised (O²⁻ at the anode). Melting or dissolving lets them move.
